report.source_text: At three months of age, we re-examined the patient using FA. The results showed that the arterio-venous anastomosis had almost completely regressed. However, chorioretinal atrophy was found at the macula and around the optic disc (Fig. 2a, b).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A Japanese infant boy, delivered at 36 weeks with fetal growth restriction and symptoms consistent with congenital CMV infection (hepatosplenomegaly, intravertebral calcification, microcephaly), was referred on day 1 of life. Systemic CMV infection was confirmed by positive CMV-DNA in urine and whole blood. Initial ophthalmological examination revealed posterior vessel dilation, a demarcation line, and arteriovenous anastomosis, but no chorioretinitis. Fluorescein angiography on day 4 showed filling delay, arteriovenous anastomosis, and a peripheral avascular zone. Ocular CMV infection was definitively confirmed by positive CMV-DNA in the aqueous humor. Antiviral therapy with oral valganciclovir was initiated around day 5 of life, leading to complete regression of vessel dilation and remarkable improvement of arteriovenous anastomosis within six days. At three months of age, follow-up fluorescein angiography showed almost complete regression of the arteriovenous anastomosis, but chorioretinal atrophy was observed at the macula and around the optic disc.

Systemic congenital CMV infection was confirmed by positive CMV-DNA in urine and whole blood.

Ocular CMV infection was confirmed by positive CMV-DNA in the aqueous humor.
Antiviral therapy with oral valganciclovir led to regression of vessel dilation and improvement of arteriovenous anastomosis.
At three months of age, chorioretinal atrophy was observed at the macula and around the optic disc, a sequela consistent with ocular CMV infection.
